links.passage: Among them we can summarize some that are particularly relevant for this work: (i) soil moisture sensors alone can be useful for determining irrigation timing, but are less useful to determine the irrigation amount, (ii) ET estimates alone may be impractical for scheduling irrigation if not backed up by dynamic assessment of the crop coefficients over time, (iii) soil evaporation calculations require knowledge of soil properties, irrigation methods and interval between irrigation and rainfall events, and (iv) information about the irrigation system (i.e., wetting area, irrigation efficiency, application rate, etc.) needs to be integrated into water requirements calculations.
supporting_passages: Indeed, Cahn and Johnson [6] pointed out several limitations of measurements, devices and methods used without a comprehensive look at the crop system.
links.inference_note: The preceding sentence attributes the list to Cahn and Johnson [6]; item (i) states that soil moisture sensors help determine irrigation timing (delivery control) but are less useful for irrigation amount.
reference_entries: Cahn, M.D.; Johnson, L.F. New approaches to irrigation scheduling of vegetables. Horticulturae 2017, 3, 28. [CrossRef]

The DSS was built to include 3 different irrigation management tools: (i) W-Tens, a field tensiometer monitoring system with a set of soil water status sensors communicating to a software; (ii) IRRISAT and (iii) W-Mod, based on the SWAP model [59] to simulate crop growth and soil water balance.
links.inference_note: The earlier sentences identify W-Tens as a tensiometer-based soil water sensing system within the DSS of Bonfante et al. [58], and the claim sentence states that W-Tens provides predictions of irrigation timing (delivery control).
